Every Thursday, the clockmaker set a bowl of water outside his shop. Nobody knew why. There were no flowers in it, no coins, no handwritten invitation. Just a blue ceramic bowl, filled almost to the rim, reflecting whatever weather the morning had brought. By evening, he always took it inside.

The baker assumed it was for dogs. The postman thought it discouraged ants. A little girl named Mara decided it was a second sky, placed low enough for small things to visit. She stopped beside it on her way home and watched clouds drift between two floating specks of dust.

One Thursday, she found the bowl empty. The shop was dark. A sign in the window said the clockmaker had retired. Mara stood there for a while, listening to the traffic. Then she borrowed a bottle of water from the baker and filled the bowl herself before continuing toward home.

Years passed. The shop became a pharmacy, then a place that repaired phones. The bowl chipped along one edge. Sometimes strangers filled it. Sometimes rain did. Once, during a bitter winter, someone knitted a ridiculous little scarf around its base. Nobody remembered who had first put it there, or quite why.

Mara, grown now, still paused when she passed. She liked that the bowl had outlasted its explanation. On warm afternoons, pigeons gathered around it, drinking with quick, suspicious movements. Then they lifted their heads, throats working, and for a moment the water settled enough to hold the whole sky again.
